body_markdown:
Medicine supply problems are continuing to affect patients and pharmacies across England, with hundreds of medicines facing availability or pricing difficulties.


The latest figures reported in September 2026 show that **243 medicines were included on the NHS price concessions list at the end of August** . The list provides an indication of medicines that pharmacies have struggled to obtain at the standard reimbursement price.


The shortages cover a broad range of treatments, including medicines for heart conditions, high blood pressure, mental health conditions, pain, diabetes, epilepsy, gastrointestinal problems and hormone replacement therapy.


Some supply problems could continue for months, with certain medicines not expected to return to normal availability until 2027.


## Why are medicines in short supply?


There are several factors that can contribute to medicine shortages. Pharmaceutical supply chains depend on manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors and pharmacies, while prices can also change significantly because of international market conditions.


In England, pharmacies generally receive a set reimbursement amount from the NHS for medicines they dispense. When the price a pharmacy has to pay to obtain a medicine rises above that reimbursement amount, the Department of Health and Social Care can introduce a price concession.


This system is intended to help pharmacies manage increased purchasing costs. However, a price concession does not necessarily mean that every pharmacy will have the medicine immediately available.


## Which medicines are affected?


The reported list contains medicines across many different categories.


Cardiovascular medicines include treatments such as ramipril, bisoprolol, candesartan, carvedilol and rivaroxaban. Several antidepressants are also included, including fluoxetine, mirtazapine, sertraline and venlafaxine.


Other medicines on the list include paracetamol, antibiotics, epilepsy medicines, diabetes treatments, HRT products, pain medicines and medicines for digestive conditions.


The source also reports serious supply protocols affecting medicines including lansoprazole, ramipril, Estradot and Creon. Under a serious shortage protocol, restrictions can apply to the quantity supplied to patients while the protocol remains in force.


## What should patients do?


If your usual prescription is unavailable, speak to your pharmacist rather than stopping treatment yourself.


A pharmacist may be able to source the medicine from another supplier or explain whether an alternative formulation or treatment needs to be considered. Where a prescription needs to be changed, the appropriate healthcare professional can advise on the safest option.


Patients should not purchase prescription medicines from unverified online sellers simply because their usual pharmacy does not have stock.


It is also sensible for people who take regular medication to request prescriptions with enough time for pharmacies to deal with potential supply difficulties.

## What does the list mean for patients?


Being included on the price concessions list does not necessarily mean that a medicine is unavailable everywhere.


Supply can vary between wholesalers and individual pharmacies, and availability can change over time. Patients should therefore check with their pharmacist if they are concerned about a particular medicine.


The situation does highlight the pressure being placed on the medicine supply chain. Pharmacists may have to spend additional time locating stock, while prescribers can face extra work when alternatives are required.


Pharmacy representatives have called for greater government action to address the underlying supply problems. The National Pharmacy Association has described shortages affecting everyday medicines as increasingly worrying and has called for a task force to tackle supply chain issues.


## Final thoughts


The continuing medicine shortage is an important issue for patients across England. The latest reported list contains medicines used for a wide range of health conditions, showing that supply problems are not limited to one particular type of treatment.


Some shortages may be temporary, while others are expected to continue into 2027.


If your regular medicine is unavailable, speak to your pharmacist or another qualified healthcare professional. Do not change your dose, stop treatment or switch to another medicine without professional advice.


### Source


**Community Pharmacy England** as the source of the price concessions list. The supplied source states that the list is updated monthly and contained 243 medicines at the end of August 2026.


### Disclaimer


This article is for general information only and is not medical advice. Medicine availability can change quickly, and being included on a price concessions list does not necessarily mean that a medicine is unavailable at every pharmacy. Patients should speak to a pharmacist, GP or other qualified healthcare professional about their individual medication. Never stop or change prescribed medication without appropriate medical advice.
